(One thing I want to mention is that this game's content warnings are for SURE necessary, and I think it's missing one very important one: [b]self-harm[/b]. This game contains some VERY graphic depictions of self-harm, and it's honestly kind of a shock that it's not included as a content warning. Please be mindful of this going into OMORI.) 

I think people are making a mistake by comparing this game to UNDERTALE. I think that's about as accurate as comparing Stardew Valley to Animal Crossing, or as comparing an apple to a ceramic statue of an apple. On first glance, they share a lot of aesthetic similarities -- but beneath the surface, they are very different games. Both OMORI and UNDERTALE have a cast of colorful characters that you are expected to interact with and gradually befriend, both have absolutely killer soundtracks, both have randomly-generated values that change minor details about the world you explore, and both feature knife-wielding, stone-faced protagonists who traverse a fantastical world while fighting strange creatures. 

But beyond that, there's not a lot in common. UNDERTALE is full of details and dialogue that gets crammed in at every corner; in OMORI, most characters will repeat dialogue if being spoken to multiple times, and the majority of the little details are in the various scares. UNDERTALE is a game where many characters are aware of things like saving, loading, and resetting; OMORI is a game where pretty much no one is aware of those things in a genuinely meta sense, although the location you save at is used in a heartbreaking way. UNDERTALE's narrator is so interesting and paints the world with such vibrant tones that they are unironically my favorite character; OMORI's is honestly kind of pathetic in comparison. Going from a world of tsundere cacti and scandalous sock drawers, OMORI's narrator saying "It's an ordinary house plant" honestly hurt. 

[b](Spoilers from here on out.)[/b]

Despite this, I think the narrator is one of the most beautiful parts of the game. At one point, the main character, Sunny, has a flashback to his childhood. (Not a PTSD flashback, although I'd argue there's plenty of those -- no, this is the kind where he's exploring his childhood home.) And the narration [i]shifts[/i]. It goes from dry, almost clinical to bursting with life. The world feels different, tilted on its axis; it is so much more alive and so much brighter than it was before he began going into long diatribes about how his sister will do his laundry for him, or about how she'll let him fall asleep next to her at night when he has a nightmare. In this version of the world, he is still twelve years old, his sister is still alive, and he is still so heartbreakingly [i]okay[/i]. 

UNDERTALE, thematically, is so broad that you can use it to discuss almost anything. There are themes of mental health, trauma, suicide, abuse, depression, and anxiety, but it is not [i]about[/i] those things. OMORI is about those things in a way that is all-consuming and unavoidable. The characters are not as immediately interesting (frankly it took me an hour to be able to distinguish between Kel and Hero), but they feel realistic. They make sense. The world is duller because it is a world clouded by Sunny's post-traumatic stress disorder, a world in which he literally cannot feel happy unless he is safe within his dreams. And even in those dreams, he is haunted by manifestations of his mistakes in the form of Stranger and a great many Somethings. The gaping pit of Black Space rests eternally beneath his feet. At a certain point in the game, running around in White Space summons apparitions of your dead sister, who vanish the instant they turn to face you. It is inescapable.

One of the best moments in OMORI finds you in a room in Black Space with your cat, Mewo, strapped to a dissection table. You are told she has been a bad girl. You assume you must cut her open to leave. But she begs you not to; you must repeatedly press "yes" to slice her open, and each time, the game describes -- in detail -- how she struggles, how desperately she [i]does not want this to happen[/i]. When I opened up the menu and realized I could stab myself, I shouted with relief. This is the absolute best way I've ever seen the urge to hurt oneself characterized. It's such a simple, yet such an understandable way, that this desire is communicated. It's more sympathetic than a great many stories that characterize it as a selfish desire, or as one blind to how good your life truly is. It's being stuck in a burning building with no way out other than a balcony; it's having a knife that you can either point at your beloved pet or at your own stomach. Sunny is not blind to the realities of his existence; in fact, he is incredibly, miserably aware of them. The game puts you in his shoes, and from them, it is so easy to see the seductive allure of flinging yourself off a hospital balcony. It is easy to decide not to go on. 

OMORI has many moments that communicate similar themes. From Kel's Comeback ability, which makes him happy and gives him a buff if he uses it while sad, to Sunny's exaggerated expressions of anger and complete inability to feel joy, to the fact that most of Omori's skills involve [i]manipulating your emotions[/i] -- it is a game about trauma. It is a game about Sunny. It is a game about being unable to walk down the stairs or see a spider without having a full-blown hallucination-inducing panic attack. It is about his friend group: the jock with a facade of happiness, the college student barely hiding his lingering depression, the delinquent with an unlivable household, his gentle best friend who ends the game with the breakdown to end all breakdowns, the looming specter of his dead sister. It is a game where the only time you can talk to a character twice without them repeating their dialogue during the tutorial is when you are about to stab yourself, a moment that I interpreted as palpable excitement and fear on Sunny's part. 

But it's also a game about recovery. You have to make the active choice to walk down the stairs, to open the door for Kel, to help Basil instead of running away. You have to choose to face the truth. In the very end, you have to choose to continue when you lose your fight to Omori. You have to choose to [i]live[/i]. 

I found, as a person with PTSD, that OMORI was a game that conveyed many of the aspects of living with it brilliantly. Fall is hard for me because seeing dead leaves in driveways reminds me of visiting my ex, and his obsession with vampires makes seeing them difficult to this day. I get mad easily, although I try very hard to mask it. And, like Sunny, I've been trapped in my own version of Mewo's room. 

OMORI is in no sense a perfect game. It railroads you in frustrating ways, most Headspace areas could be significantly reduced in size without any real harm to the game (PARTICULARLY Humphrey, Sweetheart's Castle, and Last Resort), and I personally found myself wishing that the emotion mechanic was harder or healing items were more restricted as the game went on. It's... honestly a really easy game, and the hand-holding tutorial does not help. But, in terms of storytelling, I think it's an absolute masterpiece. 

If you've read through all of this and are intrigued about the game, I would personally recommend buying it, playing up until you fall asleep after naming Sunny, and then seeing if you like the game. If you're not sold on the gameplay or the characters, either return it or watch a Let's Play until the church fight, and then decide whether or not you want the game. I found it an incredible experience and am going to be playing it again (and probably thinking about it every day for the rest of my life). But be warned: it is no UNDERTALE, and you should not go into it expecting that. Expect more of a Yume Nikki, or maybe an Ib or a Crooked Man.

Holy crap, what a rollercoaster that was. I played this completely blind. I bought Omori because of its aesthetics I saw in trailers, and psychological horror, RPG and story rich tags. I was expecting this to be one of those artsy games you play for ten hours max and then leave it, maybe come back later for a couple of achievements, but that's it. Instead I ended up finding a new favorite game going straight up to my top list, playing for almost thirty hours and also found out there's multiple endings and even new areas and bosses depending on your choices. Like holy shit, this world is MASSIVE.

Omori is work of geniuses. Characters are realistic and humane and have lots of depth, nothing is revealed too much too early, I was totally not expecting THAT, and I can only imagine what kind of mindfuck moments there's going to be when I start a new game and do things differently. Also all that foreshadowing you have no clue about during your first playthrough... ouch. [spoiler]I love how the contrast between Headspace and Faraway is portrayed. I've also had my own imagination world and even had some moments I would've rather stayed there instead returning to the real world so this hits me hard. Although you know the place isn't real, it still has its nostalgic charm you don't want to let go of.[/spoiler]

Also the game's message is probably the most important one out there: forgiveness. Our world is unfortunately full of trauma, grudge and hatred - both towards ourselves and others - and I think the most natural and fastest way out of this collective misery would be forgiveness. Not the wrong kind of "forgiveness" most people seem to think it is: just being like "eh shit happens, no big deal, I'm tough, this doesn't affect me" and wiping it under carpet only to grow something bigger and uglier and causing even more suffering. It's not even forgiveness; it's denial and belittling of both what happened and the suffering it caused.

True forgiveness is accepting the thing happened but not letting it drag you down for the rest of your life. Understanding that most bad things we cause to ourselves and others aren't intentional, but nevertheless they still happen, because we can't predict the future or we're in a situation where we have no clue of what we're doing. "Coulda, woulda, shoulda." We forget we're all human, not gods, and yet we keep subconsciously demanding we should possess knowledge and powers of a god, and unreasonably punish ourselves and each other for having neither.

Soundtrack is also pure gold. One of the best ones I've heard, and includes so many earworms.

The only downside I can come up with Omori is the absence of Steam backgrounds, avatars, emojis and stickers. This game's aesthetic is so rad I'd gladly decorate my entire profile with it.

OMORI is as incredible as it is bland. It presents itself with a very, very slow start, with gameplay that is just about passable to keep myself interested. 

I will state this here and now that I would not blame anyone for turning OMORI off even after the tenth hour. OMORI has a massive problem with too much filler content throughout its runtime that lacks any serious forward momentum. The motivation of “We have to get Basil back!” is such a cliché that I was seriously uninterested for the first few couple of hours. I was raising an eyebrow when I saved, and the game considered my 11th hour of playtime still in the prologue. 

However, the game has psychological horror elements that it keeps taunting you with, and eventually those became the main motivator to keep playing. While the slow start is annoying to go through, the game is doing it for a reason. The payoff to said horror elements is absolutely worth your time, but the important thing you must realise is that OMORI needs time to build all of it up. 
I do understand that “waiting until it gets good” is a poor excuse, but I feel in the case of OMORI, this slow build up is necessary. 

[spoiler]I think the misadventures you keep roaming around in are reflective of Sunny’s state of mind, trying to keep his only friends in life close before he moves away for good. The aimlessness is Sunny revisiting his once dear memories with friends, while suppressing his dark and depressing thoughts, trying to use his colourful headspace to lock “Black Space” away for good.[/spoiler]
The way OMORI lets these events play out feels natural and humane, which only a few games can claim.

OMORI is as bland as it is incredible. It tells an incredible, powerful emotional ride of guilt and self-doubt, where one should question themselves if they feel the same.

Contrary to what most reviews may say, OMORI is not a depressing game. It is a misunderstanding of the "post-game void" feeling that you get after finishing especially good games—which OMORI absolutely is.

OMORI is a fantastic game made by a clearly passionate studio, a love letter to the indie scene delivered through a unique art style and a soundtrack that is both memorable and haunting. All of that combined with a masterclass storytelling makes OMORI excel among indie games and games in general.

The vibrant sections of the game are all visually beautiful and well-paced. I personally didn't find any part to be particularly long; even the supposedly tiresome areas like Humphrey and the castle were by no means boring in my opinion, especially considering OMORI is a 20-30 hour long game. When it comes to the horror sequences, the game doesn't rely on cheap jumpscares to be effective. Even though there are some, the game shines by using eerie sound effects and visuals to make you feel genuinely disturbed. I want to make one thing clear immediately: Omori is absolutely NOT a game for everyone both because of the themes it touches and for some moments of the game that seem to flow apparently a bit slowly.

I think this is the only game that has given me unique emotions. In a way I feel like I've changed after playing it and i'm really glad.

[b]PLOT (there are no spoilers):[/b]
Omori deals with the story of a deep friendship between a group of friends where you will enter the shoes of 2 characters: Omori and Sunny going, as previously mentioned, to gradually touch darker and... mysterious themes.
the exploratory component and the multiple interactions of the characters with the world around them in order to join the pieces of what is happening and grasp all the aftertaste of the story will prove to be particularly important.

[b]GAMEPLAY:[/b]
In addition to the exploratory component with secret roads, events for which you will also have to often retrace the steps of the character to return to places already visited, environmental puzzles, the game has a fighting system that takes up that of the Earthbound series.

[b]CONCLUSIONS:[/b]
Unfortunately to avoid spoilers I had to omit several strengths of the game but I can venture to say that if you are players who are not in a hurry to rush a game but on the contrary prefer to continue calmly exploring, interacting with the world created and appreciating the small details and if you are not afraid of more "old style" graphics then I think this game will not leave you disappointed at all.

I spent most of my playthrough of Omori on the lukewarm end. I'm not a huge fan of traditional JRPG gameplay, and I had really only picked the game up because I liked the art style, but I was pleasantly surprised with how much I enjoyed Omori once I reached the end. 

Now, I DO think Omori has its faults, particularly: pacing in the Headspace portions of the game can really drag on too long. For me, it sucked the wind out of the sails of the overall mystery of the narrative (which you really only experience in the real world.) Additionally, at times Omori can feel like playing 2 different games, which might make sense narratively, but playing through it left me favoring one side of the game rather than the other. Granted this juxtaposition between Headspace and reality might've helped aid in how I favored one portion to another. Regardless, I wasn't a huge fan of the game up until the last act, I truly feel like Omori sticks the landing with how the story is told and how it made me feel as all the pieces fell into place. By that point I was increasingly invested and wanted to see what happened next.

Omori wasn't entirely MY type of game, though I see why people like it, and I think it's worth giving it a shot and seeing what Omocat has to tell.
